title: Pulp Fiction
synopsis: A briefcase. A boss's wife. A boxer who didn't throw the fight. You're a hitman in a bad suit. The day has, so far, been long.

nodes.text: Three kids in a Valley apartment at seven-thirty in the morning, and one of them has been holding a bag of fast food for four minutes without setting it down. Vincent keeps opening the briefcase because he likes the look people get. You take the chair. You ask the kid his name, then what he's eating, and you take your time over both. Your gun has been out the whole conversation.

choices.consequence: You do the whole passage from memory, the way you have for nine years, having never once stopped to work out what it actually says.
You skip it today for no reason you could name, and the room goes quieter than the words have ever managed to make it.

nodes.text: The kid in the back seat is answering a question nobody needed answered when the car takes a seam in the road and Vincent's gun goes off. Forty seconds later you're doing thirty-eight in a fifty on a residential street with the windows down, and Vincent is apologizing about the upholstery. It's nine-fifteen in the morning in the Valley. Every vehicle beside you sits higher than yours does.

choices.consequence: You call a friend nine minutes away whose wife gets home from night shift at ten-fifteen. That clock starts the second he says yes.
You point the car downtown with the windows down and a dead man's opinion of the traffic. Twenty-two miles of freeway in the morning glare.

nodes.text: Jimmie stands in a bathrobe saying the word divorce in a very calm voice, and the coffee he pours you is genuinely excellent, which he brings up twice. Then a man arrives in a tuxedo at eight-forty in the morning, having driven from Toluca Lake in under ten minutes, and starts assigning jobs before he has finished shaking hands. He gives you thirty minutes. He never once raises his voice.

choices.consequence: You do exactly what a stranger in evening dress tells you, including the business with the hose and the seats, and it works to the minute.
You object to his tone, get the same instruction back in the same pleasant register, and lose ninety seconds you spend all morning making up.

nodes.text: Coffee, a booth by the window, and Vincent explaining why what happened in the apartment was ordinary. You keep going back to it: six shots in the plaster behind where you were standing, and neither of you touched. He says statistics. You say you're finished — out loud, in a diner, at a quarter to ten in the morning, with syrup on the table between you.

choices.consequence: You say the word retired in front of a witness, which makes it real in a way you cannot take back over pancakes.
You let Vincent talk you into calling it a coincidence, and something goes quiet in you that you will not hear again for years.

nodes.text: Two amateurs come up out of a booth shouting — one standing on a table, one waving a gun at a waitress holding a coffee pot. Neither of them has looked at you even once. Your hand is on your piece before the manager is on his knees, and you are running an arithmetic nobody in this room can see: you stopped being this man about four minutes ago.

choices.consequence: You get the drop on him, keep your voice at breakfast volume, and turn an armed robbery into a very long conversation about everybody leaving.
You do it the way you'd have done it yesterday — fast, correct, finished — and you are still shaking when you order more coffee.

nodes.text: Switching tracks: tonight you're Vincent, and the boss has asked you, as a favor, to take his wife out while he's in Florida. Everybody in the crew has a story about a man who got too friendly with her, and no two versions match. You stop at Lance's kitchen first and get high, then drive up into the hills with the radio low, rehearsing being polite.

choices.consequence: You keep both hands visible all evening and treat her like freight you're transporting, which she clocks inside ten minutes and finds hilarious.
You decide she's a person rather than a rumor and talk to her like one, which is the last simple decision you make tonight.

nodes.text: A restaurant built inside somebody's memory: booths made of cars, waiters dressed as dead celebrities, a five-dollar milkshake she makes you taste so you can be wrong out loud. She asks a question about uncomfortable silences and then proves her own point by letting one sit there. Then they announce the twist contest, and she stands up and takes your hand and does not ask.

choices.consequence: You take your shoes off in a public restaurant for a woman you are not permitted to touch, and come home with a trophy nobody can explain afterward.
You dance badly on purpose and let her carry the whole thing, and the room watches her instead of you, which was always the safer arrangement.

nodes.text: Back at the house she puts on a record, and you go into the bathroom to give yourself the mirror speech about leaving now. Ninety seconds. In that time she has found your coat, found the bag inside the coat, read it as something else entirely, and taken a great deal of it. You come out and her nose is bleeding and she is not answering to her own name.

choices.consequence: You get her into the passenger seat and take residential streets at eighty, calling a dealer who is watching television in a bathrobe and does not want this.
You get three digits in and hang up, because the ambulance brings police and the police bring a phone call to Florida.

nodes.text: Lance's kitchen table, a medical book nobody can locate, his wife screaming about her collection, and a marker pen putting a red dot on a woman's chest. Somebody has to bring it down hard, and everyone in the room agrees it is not going to be Lance. You count to three. You come down. She sits straight up off the floor with the needle standing in her and looks around at all of you.

choices.consequence: You drive her home and agree in the car that the night was a dinner and a milkshake. Two people maintaining the same lie is nearly intimacy.
You consider telling a man in Florida what almost happened to his wife, and you are still considering it four days later.

nodes.text: Switching tracks again: now you're Butch, thirty-five, and last night you took a hundred thousand of a fixer's money to go down in the fifth and instead killed a man with your hands. Fabienne has packed the motel room. You go through the bag twice, then a third time slowly, and your father's watch — two years in a camp, and it came home — is in a drawer four miles from here.

choices.consequence: You point the car back toward a neighborhood where a man with a photograph of your face is being paid to sit and wait.
You start the engine and drive south, and the thing you left behind gets heavier every mile, which is not how objects are supposed to work.

nodes.text: The apartment is exactly as you left it. Pop-tarts standing in the toaster. And on the kitchen counter a machine gun that is not yours, which means the man it belongs to is somewhere inside two rooms. Then the toilet flushes. He comes out with a paperback in one hand and nothing in the other, sees you, and has time to arrange his face but not to move.

choices.consequence: You wipe nothing, pocket the watch, and are on the road before the pastries come up. Three minutes, door to door.
You stand over a man you never met and understand that somebody told the fixer where you'd be — which means a phone call was made about a watch.

nodes.text: A red light on a wide empty boulevard, and you are humming, actually humming, when a man crosses in front of your hood carrying coffee and a box of donuts. It's him. The man who owns your last two years. You are both looking directly at each other when your foot goes down, and the next thing either of you knows is a windshield, an intersection, and a crowd forming while you try to stand.

choices.consequence: You go at him in the street with your hands, in front of witnesses, until a shopkeeper across the road decides he has watched enough and reaches under his counter.
You get up first and manage four steps, which is when a door opens behind you and a man with a shotgun invites you both inside.

nodes.text: You come around tied to a chair in a back room smelling of gun oil and old carpet, a ball strapped in your mouth, a man opposite you in the same condition. The shopkeeper has made a phone call. His friend arrives in a uniform he is not entitled to. They flip a coin over the pair of you, take the other man through a door, and leave you with something that lives in a box.

choices.consequence: You get out of the ropes, get to the door, and then stand in a corridor listening to a man you hate being destroyed. You turn around.
You get out of the ropes and take four steps toward daylight, and those four steps are the longest walk of your entire life.

nodes.text: The front of the shop is a museum of other people's worst months: chainsaws, a hammer, a baseball bat, and above the register on a bracket a katana somebody pawned for maybe eighty dollars. You pick each one up and put it back. You take the sword because it's silent, and because holding it makes you feel like the man who survives the next four minutes rather than the one who doesn't.

choices.consequence: You go back down the stairs and finish it without a word, and it turns out quicker and considerably worse than anything you had pictured.
You come through the door holding it high and give a man in a stolen uniform two whole seconds to reconsider his life. He uses them badly.

nodes.text: He's on the floor with a towel and a look you will never forget having been allowed to see. He says the thing between you is finished — the money, the fight, all of it. Then he names the price: you leave the city tonight, you stay gone, and if anyone ever asks, neither of you was in this building. He puts out his hand. You are both bleeding on the counter.

choices.consequence: You agree to be erased from the city you were born in, and it feels less like exile than like being handed your own name back.
You push for the purse money too, which is either brave or stupid, and he laughs once from the floor and gives you half of it.

nodes.text: You come into the motel room on a chopper you didn't own an hour ago, with another man's blood down your shirt, and she is upset about the blueberry pancakes she ordered and how late you are. She has packed everything you own. She did not pack the watch, and she's standing there braced for it, small, holding a coffee cup with both hands.

choices.consequence: You tell her it doesn't matter and she can hear that you mean it, and you realize you have never once done that before, with anyone.
You let the silence work for a good ten seconds and watch her get smaller, and then you spend a year undoing those ten seconds.

nodes.text: Six-forty in the morning on a bike belonging to a dead man, with a woman on the back who has never been on one and is holding you the way people hold railings. The freeway is empty. The hills go grey, then pink, then merely ordinary. Neither of you has a plan past the county line, and neither of you has yet said the word Tennessee out loud.

choices.consequence: You check the mirror at the top of the pass and take one look at a city that is never finished with anybody, and then let it go.
You keep your eyes forward the whole way out, which is discipline, and which means you never actually said goodbye to any of it.

nodes.text: Back to the morning, back to the booth, except now you know how the rest of the day goes and the two men in the booth do not. Vincent is in the bathroom with a paperback. The coffee has been topped up three times. Across the room a young couple have been having a conversation about liquor stores that keeps getting louder, and one of them has just stood up on a seat.

choices.consequence: You keep your hand on the gun under the table and your voice completely level, and you begin by asking the man what his name is.
The old arithmetic is still in your hands — two targets, one room, under two seconds — and this morning you decide not to use it.

nodes.text: He wants the wallets in the bag with everything else, and yours goes in with the rest of them. Then he wants the case, and instead you offer him the sixteen hundred in your billfold — buying it off him, out of your own pocket, from a man pointing a gun at your face. His girlfriend is screaming from across the room. You have never in your life been this calm anywhere.

choices.consequence: You hand over everything on you and tell him it's a purchase and not a robbery, and the distinction turns out to matter to both of you.
You count it out to the dollar so he understands there are terms, and he takes it slowly, watching your hands the entire time.

nodes.text: Vincent comes back out of the bathroom into the middle of it and wants to shoot everybody, and you talk him down with two words and a look. Out in the lot he tells you the retirement thing is a phase, and offers to drive you to the meet. He will be dead inside a month and there is no way on earth for you to know that. You shake his hand anyway.

choices.consequence: You get out at a gas station on Ventura and let him pull away, and that is the last conversation the two of you ever have.
You agree to one more delivery, one afternoon, nothing complicated — the exact sentence every man in this business says before the thing that finishes him.

nodes.text: The case goes across a desk in an office above a bar, and the man who wanted it lays one hand flat on the lid and thanks you both by name. Neither of you opens it. Neither of you has ever opened it. Whatever is inside has cost four lives since Tuesday, and you notice you have entirely stopped being curious, which is new.

choices.consequence: You leave it shut and walk out with empty hands for the first time in nine years, and nobody at the door stops you.
You do the job properly, take the envelope, and let the whole thing remain somebody else's problem for the rest of time.
You do neither: you set it down, say you're finished, and walk out of a room in which nobody has ever resigned before.

nodes.text: You walk. Buses, a Greyhound, a woman in Amarillo who trades a bed for a painted fence. It takes three years and ends in a nine-table diner outside Las Cruces, where you learn eggs the way you learned everything — repetition, and refusing to be wrong twice. People drive in from town for them. Nobody in that county knows what your hands used to do, and you have stopped rehearsing the sentence that would explain it.
nodes.sceneTitle: The Path of the Righteous Man
nodes.endingTitle: The Path of the Righteous Man

nodes.text: You never do find out. Twenty years later it still surfaces at three in the morning: the weight of it, the sound the catches made. Marsellus paid you in cash and you bought an eight-unit building in Van Nuys with a bad roof. You fix the roof yourself. You are fair about deposits and quick about hot water, and every tenant you have ever had describes you, without knowing why, as extremely calm.

You stay in, because the work is the only room where you know exactly where everything is. Vincent dies in a bathroom in the spring and you carry the coffin. Marsellus retires to Palm Desert with a pool and a bad back. Somewhere in your fifties you notice you are the oldest man in every room you enter, and that the young ones go quiet when you sit down. You die in one of those rooms, mid-story, smiling.
